messages.subject: Re: CONSULTATION
messages.body_plain:
Chunlin, you don't give enough detail to comment on why your confidence
intervals were wide (and you don't give any cv's to see just how bad
they were), but usual causes of poor precision are:

1.  The animals are very aggregated, so that you detect lots on a few
lines and none on most.
2.  There are too few lines, so that variance is poorly estimated.
3.  There are too few detections.  You say that there were at least 60
sightings for each sub-population.  Do you mean more than 60 individuals
were detected, or more than 60 groups ("clusters")?  If the latter, then
small sample size should not be the main cause.

You don't say how many sub-populations you have, or how you analysed
them.  If each sub-population is a stratum in Distance, then you can
assume a common detection function (and assess whether this is a
reasonable assumption using AIC), which improves precision in estimating
the detection function.  However, it doesn't help much if the big
component of variance is the encounter rate variance.  (The output from
Distance tells you what percentage of the variance is due to estimating
encounter rate, the detection function, and mean group (cluster) size,
so this will help identify where you have a problem.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: CONSULTATION
messages.body_plain:
For problem #1 from Steve's list, one solution (for next time) is to
stratify the survey into high density and low density strata.  If this
is not possible, it's best to orient the lines (assuming systematic
parallel lines) so that each line tends to run from high to low density,
so between-line variation in encounter rate is lower.

If you did have a parallel systematic line transect design, and have a
decent sample of lines per stratum (15 or more, say), then the new
variance estimator O2 (or S1) should produce a more reliable (and lower)
estimate of variance with the data you have.  See the Distance help for
more details, Chapter 8, under Variance estimation in CDS.

Cheers, - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Chunlin:

Thank you for the additional information about your study.  The survey=20
design you employed (having between one and 3 transects per stratum). =20
This will give you a poor estimate of encounter rate variability within=20
each stratum.  In fact for strata in which you placed only a single=20
transect, Distance will report that encounter rate variance is presumed=20
to be zero (because it cannot be estimated).  By ignoring that source of=20
variability, you may find (perversely) that your smallest confidence=20
intervals are produced in those strata where you placed but a single=20
transect.

Lesson to learn:  if you wish to estimate density at the level of the=20
stratum, place enough replicate transects (15-20) within the strata to=20
produce a believable estimate of encounter rate variance within the strat=
a.

messages.subject_clean: Abstract submission now open for International Statistical
messages.body_plain:
Abstract submission now open for International Statistical Ecology
Conference.   Please visit our website for details of the conference and
other exciting developments.

http://www.ncse.org.uk/isec2010

This conference, held at University of Kent 6-9 July 2010 with this list
of invited speakers:
- Professor Lord Robert May
- Richard Barker
- Carmen Fernandez
- Jeff Laake
- Darryl MacKenzie
- Ken Pollock
- Nigel Yoccoz

In addition to invited and contributed speaker sessions, we will also be
hosting a series of workshops prior to the conference (29 June - 5
July).  Our workshop offerings include:
- Modelling Patterns and Dynamics of Species Occurrence by Darryl
MacKenzie (4 days)
- Spatially explicit capture-recapture with R by Murray Efford and David
Borchers (2 days)
- AD Model Builder by Mark Maunder and Anders Nielsen (1 day)
- Open-population capture-recapture and stopover duration models by
Shirley Pledger, Eleni Matechou and Murray Efford (1 day)
These workshops have special pricing for conference participants.

The important dates for the conference are:
- Abstract submission deadline 13 January 2010
- Notification of acceptance 17 February 2010
- Applications for bursaries (developing countries) 1 March 2010
- Early (reduced-cost) registration deadline 31 March 2010

Please visit the website to view details of the conference, speakers,
abstract submission guidelines, excursions, and workshops.  To submit an
abstract, you will need to register on the website to use the abstract
submission feature.  Note that if you were a participant in our 2008
conference, you will *not* need to register a second time for the
website (as our system will remember your username and password).
However, if you cannot remember your username and password, you will
need to register for another username.

We are excited about the upcoming conference and workshop and hope to
see you in Canterbury in July.

--
Eric Rexstad

Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews
St. Andrews Scotland KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: New paper on Distance software
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance users,

We have written a paper describing the current capabilities of the
software and giving some hints on its use.  Our goal in doing this was:
(1) to provide some useful information about the software
(2) to provide a standard peer-reviewed publication that users can cite
when referring to the software in their work

The paper has been published online today in the Journal of Applied
Ecology.  It will hopefully be in print early next year.  We have
arranged for the electronic version to be freely available online.  We
hope to host a copy locally in the future, but at present copies can be
obtained from:
http://www3.interscience.wiley.com/journal/122685866/abstract
or (direct link to pdf):
http://www3.interscience.wiley.com/cgi-bin/fulltext/122685866/PDFSTART

The citation is:
Thomas, L., S.T. Buckland, E.A. Rexstad, J. L. Laake, S. Strindberg, S.
L. Hedley, J. R.B. Bishop, T. A. Marques, and K. P. Burnham. In press.
Distance software: design and analysis of distance sampling surveys for
estimating population size.  Journal of Applied Ecology.  DOI:
10.1111/j.1365-2664.2009.01737.x

This paper should now be treated as the standard citation for the
software.  We will update the citation once it is in print (but the DOI
is an unique, permanent identifier), and also update our suggested
citation in the help pages of the Distance software with the next release.

We suggest in your write-ups you continue to be explicit about the
version and release number of Distance you used, since results may vary
between versions.  For example, you might write in a methods section:
"Analyses were carried out using Distance 6.0 release 2 (Thomas et al.
in press)"

Wishing you all the best in your distance sampling survey work,

  - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

i have a question concerning the analysis of single platform data gained
during a double platform line transect ship survey for harbour porpoises.=

During parts of the survey it was only possible to conduct single platfor=
m

.=20

rm
data, I got a g(0) for the primaries and estimated the abundance for our
study area.

 Now my question is how to include the single platform data in the analys=
is?
 I did a mcds analysis only for the single platform data and applied the

Verena

messages.subject: Re: combine single and double platform data in one analysis
messages.subject_clean: combine single and double platform data in one analysis
messages.body_plain:
Verena,

I may be off-base here (MRDS not my specialty), but if your primary
platform was doing the same thing during double and single platform
mode, then you can simply pretend to Distance that the single platform
data was actually double platform with all 0's for the tracker platform
(i.e., no trials set up).  Then, in a trial, point independence
analysis, it will get g0 from the data where trials were set up, and use
this together with all the information about shape from the primary
platform to get the full detection function estimate.  This doesn't work
for io surveys, just trial.

Please, someone who knows more than me chip in if I'm wrong...

Cheers,

  - Len

--
